title: La --- The Pronoun Carries What Left

lessons.title: la — "it," for a feminine noun
lessons.gloss: "it" for something feminine — the one word in this pair that never had to change

segments.text: Say "I have it," about the book. (Lo tengo.) Now guess the feminine version before you read on.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the form you probably guessed

segments.text: la — it, standing in for something feminine.
Hago la comida. — I make the meal. La hago. — I make it.
If you guessed la, you were not lucky. You were doing what the shape of Spanish invites you to do: el and la mark the two genders everywhere else, so the object pronouns mark them the same way.
The pronoun agrees with the noun it replaces — not with you, and not with the verb. El libro is masculine, so lo. La comida and la casa are feminine, so la.

That last point is worth pausing on. La here is not agreeing with anything present in the sentence. The noun is gone; the pronoun is carrying its gender on its behalf. This is the first time in Spanish that a word has had to remember something that is no longer being said.
Last chapter had a small mystery: why lo and not el, when both come from the same Latin word? Here that mystery quietly disappears.

The feminine object form in Latin was illam. Worn down as an article it gave la. Worn down as a pronoun it gave — la. Both routes arrived at the same place, because the vowel that got lost on the masculine side (elo becomes el) was never at risk on the feminine side.
So the masculine pair split into two shapes and the feminine pair did not. Not an exception to memorise: a single sound change that happened to bite one word and not the other.

segments.instruction: "lo tengo" then "la hago" — one syllable carries the whole difference
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "lo tengo" then "la hago" — one syllable carries the whole difference]

segments.prompt: Say I make it, about la comida.

feedback.incorrect: La hago. The pronoun takes the gender of the noun it replaces.

segments.prompt: What decides whether you say lo or la?
acceptedResponses: the gender of the noun it replaces
whether the noun is masculine or feminine

feedback.correct: Right — the noun decides, not the speaker and not the verb.
feedback.incorrect: The gender of the noun being replaced.

segments.prompt: Why does the feminine article match its pronoun exactly, when the masculine pair does not?
acceptedResponses: the masculine lost a vowel and the feminine had none to lose
the sound change only hit the masculine

feedback.correct: Exactly — one sound change, one victim.
feedback.incorrect: Both come from illam unchanged; the masculine elo lost its vowel and became el.

segments.text: Which pronoun replaces a feminine noun? (La.) What decides it — you, the verb, or the noun? (The noun, even though it is no longer there.) Next: the same slot, for the two people actually talking.
